body.text: Working from home might seem like the norm, but it's not that simple
The option to work from home (WFH) has become more commonplace for many Australian workers since 2020.
But WFH policies and expectations vary between workplaces, leaving some workers at odds with their employers.
Action over 'non-compliance' at ANZ
ANZ's latest annual report showed a steep rise in cases of workers going against the bank's WFH policy.
The ABC understands ANZ's hybrid working policy allows staff work remotely 50 per cent of the time.
The report said there were 2,204 employee relations cases involving alleged breaches of the bank's code of conduct this year, an increase of more than 600 from last year.
Of those, 139 employees were sacked, 405 received warnings and 126 left the bank.
It is unclear how many of those were related to disputes over WFH arrangements.
But the report said the increase in code of conduct breach cases was "mainly driven by an increased focus on office attendance non-compliance".
The ABC contacted ANZ for an exact breakdown of those figures, but the bank declined to comment.
Is it fair to restrict WFH days?

It is fair for workplaces to have certain requirements about working from the office, according Roxanne Hart, a workplace relations law specialist at Hart & Co Lawyers who discusses employment law cases on social media.
But this should be stated in the worker's employment contract, Ms Hart said.
This is also subject to an employee's right to make a flexible work arrangement request if they are eligible for one.
"In my view, it is fair to require staff to work from the office if that is what the business requires," Ms Hart said.
"In my own law firm, staff can work wherever they want.
"However, our work does not usually require face to face interaction.
"I believe a business should be able to decide what works for them, so long as they are up-front with employees about the requirements when they are engaged."
Do I have the right to request WFH?
That depends on your circumstances.
The Fair Work Act gives some employees the right to request flexible working arrangements, provided they meet certain criteria.
They must have worked for their employer for 12 months and:
• be a parent or caretaker of a child who is school-age or younger
• be experiencing family or domestic violence, or a member of their immediate family or household is experiencing family or domestic violence.
This also applies to casual workers, provided they have worked for their employer for 12 months on a regular and systematic basis and expect to continue to do so.
However, there is not a guaranteed right to WFH.
A workplace can refuse the request for a range of reasons, including if:
• it would be too costly for the employer
• working arrangements of other employees can't be changed to accommodate it
• it would be impractical to recruit new employees to cover the period
• it would be likely to lead to significant inefficiencies and reduced productivity
• it would significantly and negatively impact customer service.
A worker can take their dispute to the Fair Work Commission if they cannot come to an agreement with their employer, which could lead to a hearing.
How do those disputes unfold?
We asked Ms Hart about what some recent cases before the Fair Work Commission told us about how employees wanting more flexibility were faring.
She said it depended on individual circumstances and came down to how well a worker could demonstrate their need to work from home.
"Employees who have not sufficiently linked the reasons for their request to such factors have been unsuccessful," Ms Hart said.
"In addition, employees in managerial roles or in teams that require more face to face interactions have been less likely to succeed.
"Employees who have demonstrated a good work history from work over many years and who work in largely individual roles [that do not require a great deal of interaction] have had more success."
Workplaces that offer some flexibility to employees had better success defending claims than more rigid, inflexible companies, Ms Hart said.
'Onerous evidence' required

Amanda Selvarajah, a senior lecturer in business law at Monash University, said cases before the Fair Work Commission demonstrated a narrow interpretation of eligibility for flexible working conditions.

"This is counter to the spirit of the right [to request a flexible working arrangement], which was intended to promote conversations around flexible work between employees and employers," Dr Selvarajah said.

"Finding requests to be ineligible based on these onerous evidence requirements could reinforce ideas of flexible working as something that should only be offered in rare circumstances to a select few."
She said this could embolden employers not to properly consider flexible work requests when certain criteria was not met.
"Ultimately it's a shame to see organisations shy away from normalising flexibility," Dr Selvarajah said.
She wants see to a more expansive approach the eligibility criteria for WFH requests.
"This will help counter negative attitudes to flexible working given the important role flexible work arrangements play in diversifying workforces and promoting gender equality."
